question.text: Scenario: Vikram Mehta, a CFA charterholder with 7 years of experience in wealth management at a private bank, wants to set up his own investment advisory firm. He plans to register as an individual Investment Adviser with SEBI under the SEBI (Investment Advisers) Regulations, 2013. His wife Neha is an AMFI-registered mutual fund distributor who currently serves 50 clients. Vikram expects to start with 100 clients, charging an annual fee of Rs. 25,000 per client. One of his prospective clients, Mr. Rao, has assets worth Rs. 2 crore and wants both advisory and distribution services from the same family. Under SEBI IA Regulations, an individual Investment Adviser can serve a maximum of 300 clients and must apply for in-principle registration as a non-individual IA if clients exceed 300 or advisory fees collected during the financial year exceed Rs. 3 crore. A part-time Investment Adviser is limited to 75 clients. Accepted professional qualifications include CFA Charter, among others listed in the workbook. The IA must additionally hold a valid NISM Investment Adviser certification. Records of investment advice, rationale, and client interactions must be maintained for a minimum of 5 years. An annual compliance audit by a CA is mandatory. Importantly, a family member of an individual IA shall not provide distribution services to the client advised by the IA, ensuring segregation of advisory and distribution activities. Question 3 of 5: Mr. Rao wants to receive investment advisory services from Vikram and mutual fund distribution services from Vikram's wife Neha. Is this arrangement permissible under SEBI IA Regulations?

answer.text: Yes, because Neha is independently registered with AMFI and operates as a separate entity
Yes, provided Vikram discloses the family relationship to Mr. Rao in writing
Yes, because advisory and distribution are two different activities regulated by different bodies
No, because the family of an individual IA shall not provide distribution services to the client advised by the IA

explanation.text: The Logic: The workbook says that the family of an individual IA shall not provide distribution services to the client being advised by the IA. Neha, as Vikram's wife, falls within the family definition (page 338), and the segregation rule (page 350) bars her from distributing products to Mr. Rao while Vikram advises him. The Trap: Separate AMFI registration, written disclosure, or pointing to different regulators do not override the explicit family-segregation prohibition — none of these create an exception under the regulation. Note: The bar runs at the client level — the same client cannot receive advisory from the IA and distribution from the IA's family. Different clients in each track are not affected.
